I rather approve of the inherent separation of function. Prevents
wallpapering of EITHER card, and increases deck-building skill. But
interestingly, I see this split:

If you have a deck with Wakes and Deflections in it, you probably only
want to be doing that. But in a Rush crisis, or with no Deflection,
you -do- have the option to Wake and block, and the benefit always
outweighs the hand size reduction.

If you have a deck with FA's, you probably intend to only block and
haven't even put Deflections in. This puts you at a weakness against
unblockable actions since you don't have a secondary recourse. If you
HAVE put Deflections in, you can pull an expensive bounce, but I'd
usually rather lose the card slot since I operate with vampires at
about half capacity most of the time. This makes Wake still pretty
damn good, IMO.

Problem about end of current turn is the old "card dumping" argument -
I burn as many Wakes as I need to on my predator's last couple actions
and get a nice new offensive-minded hand on my untap.

I don't get it.

So you have a card (Wake) that is better for playing non-blocking
reaction cards such as Deflection - the hand size reduction is
basically meaningless since you're only playing one other card anyway,
and it was already in your hand.

And you have a different card (Forced Awakening) that is better for
blocking actions, since you can replace it immediately with one of
your cool combat cards and you're likely to play a bunch of cards
anyway.

But you don't have a card that can do both. (Anymore, at least.)

Please tell me what's wrong with this picture? I LOVE situations
where there's a trade-off. It's one of the cool things about this
game - you can make a deck that beats A, B, and C, but if D shows up,
is totally hosed. Or you can make a deck that beats A, B, and D, but
C will smoke it silly. But you can never make a deck that beats A, B,
C, *AND* D all at the same time.

I just don't see how there's an actual problem with the current
situation. At all. If you want to block with Wake, you get a little
bit of inconvenience from the no-replace clause. If you want to play
non-block reaction cards with FA, you get a little bit of
inconvenience from the extra blood burned. They work out about the
same, in practice. I only have 8 Forced Awakenings, so a lot of times
I tend to just throw Wake in my block decks so I don't have to hunt
down what deck the FAs are in - I don't recall EVER having a problem
because of the hand size, ya know?

Why is it bad that people have to pick between the two cards now?

>Why not until the end of turn?

Because GOOD free cards are a very dangerous thing to have floating
around. Cryptic Mission would be lethal if it did damage instead of
merely remove blood - you could torporize vampires at +1 stealth. Aid
from Bats is one of the most underrated cards in the game - at
*inferior*. Restoration is extremely powerful. Flash. Theft of
Vitae. Undead Strength. Immortal Grapple. Grave Robbing. Flesh of
Marble. Majesty/Earth Meld. The list goes on for quite some time.

All of these cards are free. All of them perform extremely good
effects. All of them are limited as well, by requiring a vampire with
a specific discipline. Meaning that if you want to use Grave Robbing,
you need to build a deck with Dominate, and then you need to be able
to put vampires in torpor. If you don't have a vampire with Dominate,
you can't use Grave Robbing. If your vampires with Dominate can't put
people in torpor, you may not be able to Grave Rob anyone useful.

Wake is free, performs an extremely good effect, and has no discipline
limitations. It could fit in every deck. Therefore, it needs SOME
limitation, and the current one is "replace on your untap".

If it were only "replace at the end of this turn", there is no
significant cost to Waking. More importantly, there's nothing keeping
you from putting 15 or so in your deck at minimal cost to yourself -
if you have too many in hand, play them off at the end of your
grandpredator's turn, and play the rest off at the end of your
predator's turn. Then you have a nice hand full of offensive cards,
and with 15 Wakes you know you'll be running into more soon.

>Therefore, WwEF is overcosted in front of FA,

But you still don't explain WHY you think it's overcosted. Just
saying "it is!" won't fly, and i'm afraid that's really all you're
saying with this message.

The existing relationship that we all want to maintain is as follows:

Wake is preferable when you're playing reaction cards.
Forced Awakening is preferable when you're blocking.

If you are attempting to block, a replaceable card is a Good Thing,
because you may be fishing for intercept from your deck or wanting to
draw up a cool combat card AFTER you intercept them. But either way,
since you're going to combat, you're going to be playing more cards,
so a full hand is good. FA works great here. Wake causes you to be
down a hand slot, which makes combat tricky, but functional.

It's worth noting that Bum's Rush ALSO causes you to be down a hand
slot, although only until the end of combat - so 6-card combat is
clearly workable and Wake does not cause any problems (the first time
you Wake, anyway).

But combat is also guaranteed with Bum's Rush, since a block results
in combat. (Obedience is an exception, yes.) No combat is guaranteed
by Waking, so just an end-of-combat replace is insufficient because of
the card cycling problems mentioned earlier - Wake becomes a free
card.

If you are attempting to play a reaction card, be it Delaying Tactics,
Dread Gaze, Deflection, Telepathic Counter, or whatever, FA costs you
an extra blood. Most people agree that this is pretty annoying, but a
good cost for the card. Wake merely drops you a hand slot, which is
largely irrelevant since I can't think of any two-reaction-card
combinations off the top of my head. So you play two cards from your
hand, the Wake and the Deflection, and then you replace your
Deflection. You're down a hand slot, but you didn't have to go to
combat, so it's just not a problem since you only had to play one
extra card. It's ALSO worth noting that most reaction card plays are
going to happen on your predator's turn - Deflection and Telepathic
Counter 100%, Dread Gaze and Delaying Tactics not quite 100% but
easily above 75%. So the "end of current turn" errata proposed by
many really doesn't affect Wake at all in its current form - people
who are going to wake-and-intercept their prey are going to use FA
anyway, and your prey doesn't do too many things that you'll need to
react to in a fashion OTHER than blocking.

In fact, let me pull a list of all the reaction cards, and see which
ones would conceivably apply to your prey WITHOUT blocking.

OK, out of 41 reaction cards, 19 are non-intercept and could possibly
be played during your prey's (or another vamp's) turn. Quick list:

Cardinal Sin, Failure of Mission
Cardinal Sin, Insubordination
Conflict of Interests
Deadliest Sin
Delaying Tactics
Dread Gaze
Elder Kindred Network
Eyes of the Dead
Foul Blood
Ignis Fatuus
Immaculate Vitae
Kindred Coercion
Legacy of Power
Malkavian Rider Clause
Mistaken Identity
Political Backlash
Pulling Strings
Surprise Influence
Treachery

All the other cards gain intercept in some form or specify "your
predator" as the target; for example, Tainted Vitae is only usable
when your predator's vampire hunts. I also removed Forced Awakening,
Wake, and 2nd Tradition from the list, though they're reaction cards -
for obvious reasons.

Going through that list, a number of cards can be found that are
EXTREMELY rare to be seen at all, either due to overly restrictive
playing conditions (Mistaken Identity) or just plain suck-o-rama (Eyes
of the Dead). If we remove both Cardinal Sins, Conflict of Interests,
Eyes of the Dead, Immaculate Vitae, Legacy of Power, and Mistaken
Identity, we have only 12 cards left.

Of those 12 cards, 10 are related to votes. Deadliest Sin is an
anti-diablerie card, and Foul Blood is an anti-hunt card. Only one
card is dependent on you playing a vote deck yourself - Malkavian
Rider Clause. All the others depend on another deck calling votes
somewhere on the table for you to affect, which is not guaranteed at
all. If it's not your prey (very likely), it may not be to your
advantage to even PLAY the cards.

So most of the time, the reaction cards you include in your deck are
going to be either intercept, or defense against your predator. With
this in mind, the suggested errata "replace at end of current turn"
really begins to make no sense at all. In fact, it makes no sense to
alter the current form of the card, since there should be a LARGE cost
to tapping to take an action against your prey, and then Waking to
affect his actions as well - this should oust your prey VERY quickly.

The suggested errata of "burn a blood if you fail to block or play a
reaction card" makes the card too much like Forced Awakening, which is
not good. Some decks include light intercept to use against their
prey's or predator's actions, and Deflections/TMs to use against their
predator's bleeds. Currently, you would want to play a Wake in this
deck since you don't know if you're going to need to untap for your
prey or predator. For the flexibility of tapping out taking actions,
stopping some of your prey's critical actions, AND defending against
your predator all at the same time, you have a greater and appropriate
cost - don't replace until your untap. Again, it comes down to
choices, and tapping all your vamps out should NOT be the default
choice just because "they can always Wake".

opportunity to stop your prey's deck from doing its thing as WELL as

Intercept tends to fail because of several reasons.

One, it's too reactive. Your prey will generally take a number of
bleed actions during the game. Those actions cannot be blocked by you
without Eagle's Sight. This puts a real cramp in your intercept deck,
especially once your prey realizes that he's "safe" from you as long
as he just keeps going forward - which makes him oust his own prey
faster. Which means you oust him probably not at all. So a
successful intercept deck MUST use superior Auspex and include a
number of Eagle's Sight cards.

Two, it requires a significant deck-space investment to be able to
stop most actions. A good base number to shoot for is +3 intercept -
this allows you to stop a Lost in Crowds + Cloak the Gathering, and
will keep you out well ahead of most actions, except against a
heavy-stealth deck. Unfortunately, it is easier to generate stealth
than intercept, so intercept tends to lose.

Three, you have the Dog and the Mail Truck problem - what do you do
when you catch them? To oust your prey, you need to remove his
resources, so you generally want to kill them. This means you need
some sort of WAY to kill them, not something that Auspex clans outside
the Tzimisce specialise in. Tremere combat is too card-intensive to
mix with good intercept, and the Malks and Toreador have to rely on
guns. Guns are expensive, putting another thorn in the interceptor's
side - he now has to include enough blood gain to pay for his
weaponry.

Four, once you kill all your prey's vamps, how do you oust him? More
deck space, and/or a bunch of small bleeds.

Five, how do you do 1-4 without BEING ousted? More deck space and
LOTS of untap cards since you'll be tapped out from blocking or
bleeding your prey.

Notice something? The untap (wake/FA) problem doesn't come into play
until WAY down near the tail end... on your predator's turn. The real
problems with intercept decks succeeding don't lie with the untaps at
all - Guard Dogs/Rat's Warning are excellent cards, and Cat's Guidance
at inferior is tailor-made for ANY intercept deck - why would you FA
*or* Wake when you can CG on the action before?

The problems are when you try to make a deck that can stop things,
beat things up, and then bleed forward as well. It's three deck types
combined into one, and it is very hard to make work - you usually end
up having beat-things-up cards in hand instead of intercept when you
need it. Or you have only lots of intercept and your vamp gets beat
up instead of the other guy first time you stop something.

> Yet WwEF is still commonly played. It seems that the players do not agree
> with this theory of overcosting.

I've now heard this argument enough that I felt I had to respond. Just
because a card continues to be played doesn't mean the errata on it is
good or that that it couldn't be improved. All it means is that it hasn't
been turned into wallpaper. It doesn't mean everyone using the card is
nodding their heads and saying "Oh yes, this card is exactly appropriately
costed now."

For example, many people feel that the errata on Tomb of Ramses is overly
harsh. You will, however, see it played on infrequent occasions. Tomb
of Ramses got turned from an overly-good card into an extremely marginal
card. Most people would have preferred to see it turned into a "just good
but not overly good" card.

The people arguing against the current Wake errata feel the card is
excessively penalized, not that it has been turned into wallpaper.

BTW, I don't even necessarily feel that the current errata is overly harsh.
However, it is an awkward mechanic (typically requiring some kind of memory
aid to avoid prematuring redrawing) and could in all probability be
improved.

It didn't become complete wallpaper, no. There is a whole spectrum of
strengths between "overpowered" and "wallpaper" you know. I don't
necessarily agree that unerrataed Wake was even overpowered. However,
the free cycling was a problem in that it went against one of the basic
design principles of the game (that the discard phase is a limited resource).
I imagine this was also one of the motivations for the "no vote pushing"
rule [rather than some alternative fix for weenie vote pushing].

People on the "other side" of this thread would typically like an errata
that patches the 'free cycling' problem without adding additional penalties
on the use of Wake. As I see it, the 3 main problems with the current
errata are:

1) It is tedious to keep track of exactly what your hand size is
over the course of several turns, particularly if you get in a
frequent-card-drawing situation (e.g. combat).

2) Wake, without cycling, wasn't demonstrated to be overpowered.
There was no justification for adding an additional penalty to
the card beyond stopping cycling.

3) It makes some problematic cards, such as Misdirection, even
worse. It is hard enough to fight weenie Dominate tap-and-bleed
with unerrataed Wake. With no card redrawing until the next turn,
it becomes very much harder.

> becoming wallpaper is okay? I hope not.

Of course not. However, it is an influencing factor. People are still
using it, people are still using it in preference to Forced Awakening, and
it is still played. These are factors which suggest (but do not
dictate) that the errata is fairly balanced.

> Your loyal opposition is arguing
> that the errata to Wake went beyond what was necessary to fix the problem
> (cycling) and excessively hobbled the card.

Clearly, I do not agree.

I have stated, and will state again, that there are no circumstances under
whcih I believe the 'perfect' errata will ever be found for any
over-powered card. There are always different conflicting factors that
all merge in on a piece of errata which no one errata can ever satisfy
perfectly. For instance, the original intent is a factor, play balance in
the current set and possibilities (these first two often conflict),
simple to remember, a useful explanation (these last two can go hand in
hand, if there is a 'story' behind the errata) and so on. Clearly, player
reaction is an other factor to consider, but it is not the *only* factor -
simply because you cannot guarantee how all or even a sizeable portion of
players will react. Tehre have been errata which I expected to see many
more complaints about, but didn't get, and vice versa.

I can see that, to appease other factors, removing the errata will improve
those other areas - but it will conflict in other areas, too. In this
instance, the factor I believe is paramount is play-balance - and I
believe the card is very balanced. If it was so overly expensive, Fored
Awaekning would be all the rage amongst those players who can use it, or
JOL. This does not seem to be the case.

>
> It didn't become complete wallpaper, no. There is a whole spectrum of
> strengths between "overpowered" and "wallpaper" you know.

Of course. I believe that Wake originally occupied the position of
"overly useful, and overly cheap". I believe it now occupies "balanced".

> design principles of the game (that the discard phase is a limited resource).
> I imagine this was also one of the motivations for the "no vote pushing"
> rule [rather than some alternative fix for weenie vote pushing].

IMO, that (violating basic principles) would move towards fulfilling, in
my mind, one possible definition of overpowered (since there will be
different definitions for different situations). Again, it wouldn't be
the only factor - but it is a factor, I feel.

> 1) It is tedious to keep track of exactly what your hand size is
> over the course of several turns, particularly if you get in a
> frequent-card-drawing situation (e.g. combat).

I find that simply keeping the Wake in my other hand, or placing it (as
with other Do Not Reaplce cards) on the table in front of me, removes such
tedium.

>
> 2) Wake, without cycling, wasn't demonstrated to be overpowered.

> There was no justification for adding an additional penalty to
> the card beyond stopping cycling.

This errata does stop card cycling. Note that some of the alternatives
put forward do other things - like showing other people the cards - or
simply speed up the time (under some cirucmstances) in which the card is
replaced (e.g. if you successfully block etc.)

> worse. It is hard enough to fight weenie Dominate tap-and-bleed

Etrius can be a bad, bad man - his disciplines lend themselves to that
sort of thing (AUS/DOM/OBF is nothing to sneeze at, and if he feels
like fighting, he does have THA). Gwendolyn's POT/FOR is great if you
minion tap her, since she can Taste back a bunch of blood very quickly
- but she has no Dominate. Leandro is only good because of his
special - the Dominate problem again. Alexandra shows up for her
"free action" special, so even though she's short on Dominate it
doesn't hurt much.

Harrod's problem (and to some degree, most ICs' problems) is that his
disciplines (POT OBF CEL ANI aus pre) are all eclipsed by other IC
members *or* by plain old cheap vampires. POT/CEL/PRE comes on
Gwendolyn and a lot of Brujah, so scrap those discipline combos right
there. OBF/XXX is neat but you can get it much more cheaply, and
three other IC members have it. POT/ANI is found on Nigel and others.
Why you'd want OBF/ANI I'm not sure but it's definitely out there lots
cheaper. CEL/ANI is on Stanislava and Alexandra. POT/AUS is on
Sheldon. And on top of it all, Harrod has no Dominate.

I beat on the Dominate angle so much because that's a strong way for
IC members to pay for themselves without having access to 5th
Tradition - they can use Govern to pull out every other member of your
crypt on the cheap. And sure enough, the guys with DOM are the ones
you see most - Arika and Stanislava.

>The best thing about weenies is that they're disposable. I can't see big
>vamps as disposable short of the Redeem The Lost Soul deck (*giggle*). The
>second best thing about weenies is they come out fast and in quantity.
>Fast, TOR3 handles. In quantity? Freak Drive, Rutor's Hand, other things
>that allow a big vamp untappy fun sure help, but are costful and very

The *best* thing about weenies is that they provide lots of actions.
Compare: I have Arika out. I drop two cards and bleed for 8, and
drop a third to do it at +2 stealth. If I don't Freak Drive (fourth
card), I can do nothing else that turn, and if I want to do something
else instead, I can't bleed for 8.

Now, I have four weenies out. I play a Misdirection to tap you, and
drop four Computer Hackings to bleed for 8. Two extra cards, so the
big vampire's mondo discipline barrage is more efficient. But I have
all kinds of flexibility with the weenies. I can bleed for 6 and send
a weenie to steal the Rack. I can bleed for 4, get a Rack, and
diablerize someone's 10-cap. I can do this with Arika too, but I need
two Freak Drives and it starts to cost me a good chunk of blood
(govern + condition + 2 freak drives = 4 blood spent this turn, as
opposed to the weenies who have spent nothing). I also need to be
sure that I can pass the bloodhunt vote, since losing Arika to
diablerie would be a real pisser. Losing a weenie is worth it to fry
a 10-cap, usually.

When it comes down to it, four actions per turn will do better than
one action per turn. Freak Drive helps this for big vamps, and it's
not surprising that the common ICs, Stanislava and Arika, just happen
to have FOR - and the only other IC with FOR is Gwendolyn. Alexandra
shows up a lot because she has a built-in Freak Drive (usable on
others).

We aren't even going to go into defense - drop Hostile Takeover,
Pentex Subversion or Sensory Deprivation on Arika, and poof - kiss
your deck goodbye. Try that on a weenie deck sometime and see what
happens - the Pentex goes away on the first turn, and the SD vamp
turns into the primary choice for wake/suicide defense, or
wake/deflect. Hostile Takeover is GREAT for a weenie deck - pool gain
for a used vampire! Meanwhile, the weenie deck has barely been slowed
down. And god forbid Arika get caught without Obedience by weenie
Rush - Grapple, Undead Strength, Disarm, and the next weenie
diablerizes. Poof! (Although with FOR she ought to be preventing if
she's not Obediencing, but we're all familiar with "deck screw" and
having none in hand and 10 in the library.)

Any cards that are to help big vampires are going to HAVE to address
the multiple-action issue first, or it will be pointless. RtI tried,
but all that did was create the "Hot Potato of Death" deck as people
discovered new and exciting ways to include 12 Deflections. Kindred
Coercion is good, but it's rare, requires Dominate, and is a defense,
not an offense. There are maybe a couple others, but they come up
against the same problem - how do you compare to all four actions?
The only other possible solution is to make a big vampire's actions
more effective than a 2-cap with a skill card's, and that involves
printing a bunch of age-related cards, and it might just be easier to
find ways to give big guys more actions. Maybe a disciplineless
variant of Freak Drive, only usable by a vampire of 9 capacity or
higher. But that makes some ugly 5th Tradition combos possible with
the huge Princes - Minion Tap, 5th, Freak Drive, take offensive action
with suddenly-free vampire. That's already powerful, I don't know
that we need to give it to the non-FOR guys. =)

>Hmmm... cards with the equivalent of inferior and superior effects dependent
>on age? How would that interact with disciplines, I wonder?

-shrug- Put a Dominate symbol on the card. Card text: "Bleed at +1
stealth. If the acting vampire is capacity 9 or greater, this action
is also for +2 bleed."

Obviously, this card would be a terrible, TERRIBLE new addition, but
it serves its purpose as a quick example of how it could work. =)
Several discipline cards already have no inferior/superior versions -
Army of Rats, Horrific Countenance, etc.

Or maybe an action modifier that provided the effects like Camarilla
Exemplary - "Any younger vampire must burn 2 blood when attempting to
block this action." Or a free OBF card like Forgotten Labyrinth, but
that was tied to capacity instead of inferior/superior. Or Or Or...
you get the picture. It'd be possible to go through the disciplines,
find a "good" card for each, and rewrite it slightly to be
average-weak for weenies, but better than the "good" card for 9-caps
and up. Protean could have free claws. Celerity could get "Maneuver.
(9) Maneuver, with an additional strike this round." Auspex could
have "+1 intercept. (9) +3 intercept." The possibilities become
quite varied. =)
